label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**One assignment**

Jess texted me last night, and half of you agreed with her in the group chat, so I'm writing this instead of sending fifteen texts I'd regret by the fourth one. This is for all of you, but it's mostly for Jess. Jess, I'm not mad. I knew you'd say it, and if our places were swapped I'd probably have said it too.

Here's what happened, for those who've only gotten the group-chat version.

Every fall my juniors in US History II do an oral history project. Two sections this year. Each kid interviews someone in their family or their neighborhood about busing in Boston, 1974 to 1976: the desegregation order, the buses, the rocks, all of it. They bring back a ten-minute recording and write a two-page reflection. I've done it four years at Cobb Street and never had a single complaint.

A couple weeks ago a parent emailed my principal and cc'd someone on the school committee. She said the project "reopens wounds" and "pressures kids to judge their grandparents." My principal called me in and, in the nicest possible way, suggested I let it go quietly this year. Skip it, nobody needs to make a thing of it. There's a meeting Thursday the 19th at 3:15 with the two of us and the parent.

I'm not going to drop it. That's the short version. The rest of this is the why.

---

First, the parent, because I don't want anyone reading this as me gearing up for a fight with her. I'm not. I think she has a point, and it's the part about pressure. When a sixteen-year-old's teacher tells them to go interview their family about something ugly, that isn't a neutral request. There's a grade on it. There's me. Some kids have a grandfather who was in the crowd in Southie, or a grandmother who still won't talk about why the family moved to Quincy in '75, and I'm sending them home to ask about it. I've always known that, but I'll admit I thought about it less than I should have because nobody had complained.

So here's what I'm bringing Thursday. The project stays, and it gets an alternate track. Any kid who doesn't want to interview family can interview a librarian or archivist (the BPL people are great, and so are the folks at UMass Boston), or they can work from recordings past students made, with those students' permission. Same reflection, same grade weight. No kid has to sit across from their grandparents. I think that's what she's actually asking for, even if her email asked for more.

That's the line for me. The kids who are uncomfortable are often the ones who'd get the most out of it, and I believe that. But I don't get to force anybody. Those two things are both true, and the alternate option is how I'm trying to hold both.

---

The question underneath your text, though, Jess, is why I'd bother. It's one assignment. Why not drop it this year, let things cool off, and maybe bring it back later?

Partly it's that it's not really one assignment. It's the history of the city these kids live in. They walk past these schools. Some of them ride the same routes. The textbook gives it a paragraph, one, sandwiched between Watergate and the energy crisis like it happened somewhere else. If I drop it, the paragraph is all they get, and I don't think that's an exaggeration. Nobody else in the building is teaching it. If it's not this, it's nothing.

The bigger reason is that I've seen what happens when they do it.

In 2023 a kid I'll call D. interviewed his grandmother. Turned out she drove a school bus in South Boston in 1974. She'd never told anyone in the family. Not her kids, not her husband, not really. She told D. because he asked and because he had a phone recording and a due date, which gave her a reason. He played about forty seconds of it for the class. She's describing pulling up to the school and what people were yelling and how she kept her eyes on the mirror. When it ended nobody said anything for close to a minute. Juniors. A full minute of silence, in a room of sixteen-year-olds, at 1:40 in the afternoon. I've been teaching fourteen years and I can count those moments on one hand.

Last year a girl found out her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus. She came to me after class really upset. Not crying exactly, more like she didn't know what to do with her face. We talked that day and again later that week. I didn't tell her what to think about him. I'm not sure I'd have known what to say anyway. She worked it out in the reflection, which was about how you can love someone and know that about them at the same time, and what you owe the people on the bus. It was the best thing I read all year. Not the best student writing. The best thing.

So when the email says the project "reopens wounds," I don't think it's wrong, exactly. I think the wounds are already there, and this is one of the few places a kid gets to look at them with an adult nearby who's paying attention, instead of finding out at Thanksgiving when they're twenty-five and someone's had too much wine.

---

You're not wrong that I could get burned. I want to say that clearly so it doesn't sound like I'm brushing you off. I've been tenured since 2021, so nobody's firing me over an oral history project. But my principal still controls my schedule and who gets AP, and there are a hundred quiet ways a year can get worse that never show up in writing. You did HR long enough to know exactly how that works, probably better than I do.

And I'm a little scared. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. This isn't me being brave. I've thought about just doing what she asked, and some nights it's sounded pretty good. I like my job. I like teaching AP. I'd like a calm spring.

But I keep picturing next fall, standing in front of two sections of juniors, teaching that one paragraph, and knowing why. Knowing there's a D. in the room whose grandmother drove a bus and will never tell anyone now. I don't think I could do that and still feel like the teacher I was trying to be when you and I were student teaching in 2012, making photocopies at 6:45 and swearing we'd never become the burned-out ones in the faculty lounge.

You left in 2019 and you were right to. You're happier, and I've watched it. I don't think staying makes me better than you, and I don't think leaving makes you wrong about this. You looked at the situation and saw risk, which is your job now, and honestly it's the job of a good friend. I looked at it and saw D.'s grandmother. We're probably both right.

---

I'm not asking anyone to agree with me. I just didn't want you to think I hadn't heard you, or that I'm doing this out of stubbornness, or because I like a fight. (Okay, Jess, you've known me fourteen years. Not *mostly* because I like a fight.)

I'll go into the meeting Thursday, listen to her, offer the alternate option, and try hard not to be defensive. Maybe it goes fine. Maybe it doesn't.

Either way, I'll text you after. Probably around 4:30, probably from the car, probably before I've decided how I feel about it. Have your phone on.

---

That's around 1,350 words. One change from your notes: I left out your principal's name and just said "my principal." It's a small blog, but it's public and searchable, and if this somehow reaches the school committee member who was cc'd, you probably don't want Dr. Halvorsen named in a post published before the meeting. If you'd rather name him, it's easy to put back.
